newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Court extends asset freeze on ex-Yugoslavia.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Court extends asset freeze on ex-Yugoslavia.

text.p: A Paris court on Tuesday extended a freeze on assets of former Yugoslavia held in French banks despite opposition by Belgrade, a lawyer said.

The court also ordered French banks to give details within two weeks of any deposits or withdrawals on the accounts since the end of 1990, said Christian Feddal, a lawyer acting for Croatia, Macedonia and Bosnia.

The three states and Slovenia had pushed for the freeze and account details, fearing that rump Yugoslavia -- Serbia and Montenegro -- would otherwise exert sole control over assets estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars.
"The four countries have won the freeze they wanted," Feddal told Reuters. Banks would face financial penalties if they failed to comply. Rump Yugoslavia had opposed the continued freeze.

After the break-up of Yugoslavia, triggering the worst fighting in Europe since World War Two, all assets of the former federation held abroad were frozen in line with a U.N. resolution which expired last November.
The four states want all assets frozen until the countries formally agree how to split up the assets held by the former Communist state.
Feddal said the four countries suspected there had been withdrawals from the accounts since December 31, 1990 despite the U.N. freeze. "This ruling will help us find out," he said.
The head of the Slovenian Succession Fund, Andrej Rant, estimated last week that there were about $590 million of former Yugoslav assets in nine French banks.

The banks are Societe General, Paribas, Credit Commercial de France, Banque Francaise du Commerce Exterieur, Credit Agricole, Banque Nationale de Paris, Banque Commerciale pour l'Europe du Nord, Credit Lyonnais and Banque Franco-Yugoslave.
Feddal said eight of the banks left it up to the court to decide whether to extend the freeze. The Banque Franco-Yugoslave wanted the accounts unfrozen.
But all, apart from Credit Lyonnais, had opposed disclosing details of the accounts, arguing publication would violate French bank secrecy laws.
The bulk of the former federation's assets, about $660 million, is held by the Basle-based Bank for International Settlement (BIS).

The central banks of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Macedonia have backed a BIS proposal to split up the assets in line with a formula proposed by the International Monetary Fund which would give Slovenia, for instance, a 16.39 percent stake.
